I'm picking a test drop that sits outside the smoke, so the wind reading isn't skewed by the updraft, and settling on a release at altitude 100, heading 90, speed 60, at x=0, y=-200.

I'm checking the wind speed and direction at 100 m, along with the measured fall time of 7.11 s. Without drag the fall would take about 4.52 s, so the longer time suggests drag is slowing it down. Quadratic drag depends on the air-relative velocity, so the vertical motion should contribute to it as well.

Now I'm working out the drag coefficient: a terminal velocity near 15.7 m/s at 0.04 would match an average fall speed of about 14 m/s over the 100 m. That puts the drag somewhere in the 0.03 to 0.05 range. Next I'm checking the horizontal and vertical drift against the wind vector, and planning drops at 40 m and 150 m to measure shear.

I'm settling on a test drop at 40 m on the same heading, to pull out wind shear near the surface. I'll also plan drops inside the smoke to look for updrafts and measure fall times at different altitudes.

I'm working out the wind shear from the speed drop between 40 m and 100 m: the ratio of 4.7 to 6.2 gives a shear exponent of about 0.30. With roughly 0.5 m/s of noise, I'd put the shear somewhere around 0.2 to 0.4. I'm also noting that the wind direction turns from 52 at 40 m to 32 at 100 m, a veer.

I'm checking the veer against the direction readings, which comes out to about -33 degrees per 100 m, give or take 10. I'm planning a 150 m drop outside the smoke to get more shear and veer data.

Now I'm fitting a wind-speed profile: I'll test a shear exponent of 0.3 and 0.2 against the readings and find that a value near 0.2 to 0.25 with a mean speed around 6.3 m/s fits best. For direction, the veer is roughly 25 degrees per 100 m, which puts the wind direction near 30 degrees at 100 m. I'm also noting the fall times at each height, where the drag-driven spacing between 100 m and 150 m differs from the spacing between 40 m and 100 m, and I'm planning to fit a drag model to those next.
